{{Short description|5th century Neoplatonic philosopher}}
{{for|the Italian saint|Saint Marinus}}
{{use dmy dates|date=July 2020}}
'''Marinus''' ({{langx|grc|Μαρῖνος ὁ Νεαπολίτης}}; born c. 440&nbsp;AD) was a [[Byzantine]] [[Neoplatonic]] [[philosopher]], mathematician and [[rhetorician]]{{sfn|Edwards|2000|p=55, n.3}} born in [[Nablus|Flavia Neapolis]] (modern Nablus), [[Palaestina Secunda]]. He was a student of [[Proclus]] in Athens. His surviving works are an introduction to [[Euclid]]'s ''[[Data (Euclid)|Data]]''; a ''Life of Proclus'', and two astronomical texts. 

Most of what we know of his life comes from an epitome of a work by [[Damascius]] conserved in the Byzantine [[Suda]] encyclopedia.{{sfn|Edwards|2000|p=55}}

==Life==
He was, according to his pupil Damascius, born a [[Samaritan]].{{sfn|Luz|2017|p=150}}{{efn|'He says that the successor of Proclus, Marinus, came from Neapolis in Palestine, a city situated near the mountain called [[Gerizim|Argarizon]] Then the impious writer uttered the blasphemy that on this mountain there is a most holy sanctuary of Zeus the Highest, to whom Abraham the father of the old Hebrew consecrated himself'. ''Vita Isadori'', 141. {{harv|Mor|2016|p=376}}}} Whether this information is correct is disputed, but it is quite possible. Damascius also adds that he had converted from [[Samaritanism]].{{sfn|Hartmann|2018|pp=188-191}}

He came to [[Athens]] at a time when, with the exception of [[Proclus]], there was a great dearth of eminent men in the [[Platonic Academy|Neoplatonist school]]. He was appointed as successor (''[[wikt:diadochos|diadochos]]'') to Proclus, sometime before the latter's death, during the period of the teacher's infirmity. Proclus dedicated to Marinus his commentary on [[Plato]]'s [[Myth of Er]].<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Carine|last1=van Liefferinge|url=https://www.cairn-int.info/article-E_RHR_2294_0479--sirens-from-the-deadly-song-to-the-music.htm|title=Sirens: From the Deadly Song to the Music of the Spheres. Homeric Readings and Platonic Interpretations|volume=229|issue=4|date=October 1, 2012|access-date=May 18, 2021|journal=Revue de l'Histoire des Religions|language=English, French|doi=10.4000/rhr.7980|issn=0035-1423|oclc=828551875|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Proclus himself, it is reported, worried that Marinus himself was of delicate constitution.{{sfn|Edwards|2000|p=56, n.7}} During this period, the professors of the old [[Religion in ancient Greece|Greek religion]] suffered persecution at the hands of the Christians and Marinus was compelled to seek refuge at [[Epidaurus]], where he died, at a date unknown.{{sfn|Edwards|2016|p=1}}

==Works==
Only a remnant of his output survives.{{sfn|Edwards|2016}} His chief surviving work was a biography of Proclus, since it is the main source of information on Proclus' life. This was written in a combination of prose and epic [[hexameter]]s, of which only the former survives.{{sfn|Edwards|2016|p=1}}

The publication of the biography is fixed by internal evidence to the year of Proclus's death; for he mentions an [[eclipse]] which will happen when the first year after that event is completed. It was first published with the works of [[Marcus Aurelius]] in 1559; it was republished separately by [[Johann Albert Fabricius|Fabricius]] at Hamburg in 1700, and re-edited in 1814 by [[Jean François Boissonade de Fontarabie|Boissonade]] with emendations and notes.{{sfn|Wagner|1840|pp=204–205}} He is also the author of a commentary (or introduction) on the ''[[Data (Euclid)|Data]]'' of [[Euclid]], and a commentary on [[Theon of Alexandria|Theon]]'s ''Little Commentary''.{{sfn|O'Connor|Robertson}} There is also a surviving astronomical text which discusses the [[Milky Way]].{{sfn|O'Connor|Robertson}}

His lost works included [[commentaries on Aristotle]], on [[Theon of Alexandria]] and on some of the dialogues of [[Plato]]. He is said to have destroyed his commentary on Plato's ''[[Philebus]]'' on the advice of a pupil he was tutoring, [[Isidore of Alexandria|Isidorus]].{{sfn|Hartmann|2018|pp=196-203}} According to a version of the story written by Damascius, when Marinus showed his student, to whom he taught [[Aristotelianism]],{{sfn|Edwards|2000|p=56}} this commentary, which he had just completed, Isidorus prevailed on him to destroy it, arguing that since the 'divine' Proclus had himself written a definitive commentary which was the final word on the topic.{{sfn|Trust|2014|p=133}} Current scholarship suspects that this advice arose from fears that Marinus' commentary would, despite his best efforts, betray traces of material that might undermine the reigning [[Neoplatonism|Neoplatonic]] [[paradigm]].{{sfn|Trust|2014|p=133}}
